beats.say: Imagine a world where Britain's red flag stitched onto deserts, jungles, and icy tundras alike.
beats.visual: British flag planted on desert dunes 19th century

beats.say: By 1884, the Berlin Conference carved Africa into British zones, but the map omitted a hidden enclave.
That speck was the tiny protectorate of Zanzibar, a strategic port controlling Indian Ocean spice routes.
In 1900, Britain leased the distant island of Heligoland from Germany, swapping it for African claims.
The map's oddity shows a British enclave inside the Ottoman Empire: the Dodecanese islands, seized in 1912.
Yet the most shocking omission was the 1916 British-run railway across the Sahara, linking Morocco to Egypt.
This iron spine moved troops faster than any camel caravan, reshaping colonial logistics forever.
When the empire fell after 1947, the railway was dismantled, its tracks vanished beneath desert sands.
Today, only faint outlines remain on vintage maps, a ghostly reminder of Britain's hidden arteries.
